content:
I've recently guided Claude (Opus 5.5) to find a polynomial time algorithm for the two-path Zig Zag Numberlink problem (source: R2K2ZZN). The proof is Lean verified and I think would be a good candidate to submit to the registry but there are 154 native_decides needed because of heavy case analysis. My understanding is that the native_decides precludes it from being submitted to the registry.

Are there any other options to try to get this proof into the registry? Would it be possible to make an exception? Are there any other suggestions on how to proceed?

Hi @Zzyv Zzyzek

I think the community has a strong view against native_decide , unlike decide it will bypass trusted kernel approach and relies on c code compiler. An automated check can easily miss false proof or exploit.

What about by decide + kernel instead how much time is it taking, if you keep recurssion shallow and split into multiple files it might work? You may ask claude to provide with alternatives to native_decide
Issue with native_decide was documented in this thread: #Palomar > con-ron kernel rejected the solution .

con-ron rejects native_decide because it introduces new axioms . con-ron also rejects mutually inductive definitions. So to the extent people use Palomar, they will need to avoid features which are not in the con-ron dialect, including any such uses if they occur in Mathlib.

I did ask Claude about alternatives for the very reason I wanted to submit to Palomar. My understanding is the case analysis was just so large that doing just decides were, if not out of the question, very costly.

I'll review with Claude to see. Maybe it can be done with decides only at the cost of some not-unreasonable amount of compute.

The question then becomes, if it were transferred to only decides, and the run was 24+ hours of compute to run, would Palomar be able to handle such a case?
@Zzyv Zzyzek Palomar has a execution runtime budget set at 5 hours and 30 mins, and I dont think one can override this for builds. Let us know if you are able to solve this.

The proof is "brute force", so heavy on the case analysis which is why the runtime is so large. I'm loathe to try to optimize further because it's conceptually simple, but it comes at the cost of enumerative case analysis which costs runtime and precludes it from things like Palomar.

There are maybe ways of optimizing the proof. If I pursue further, I'll let you know how it goes.
